    E02 — A single-family house: foundation earth electrode in concrete¶

    This case study models the earth of a detached single-family house: a foundation earth electrode in the concrete of the strip foundation, optionally with a driven rod or a ring earth electrode outside the foundation. It is written for the grounding engineer who wants to know what such an earth achieves, how much the concrete and the soil change it, and which of groundfield's engines to trust for which answer.

    The questions

    1. What is the earthing resistance of the house, and how much do the concrete and the soil model change it?
    2. What do people around the house experience when its earth rises in potential: the potential profile, the touch voltage at the façade and the step voltage?
    3. What does a driven rod or a ring earth electrode outside the foundation add?
    4. What do the engines image / image_2layer, mom and fem give for this house, and why do they differ?

    Prerequisites: the tutorials T01, T02, T08 and T09, and the page Concrete-encased electrodes. Runtime: about half a minute. An optional three-dimensional fem run near the end takes one to three minutes and up to 3.5 GB of memory more; it is switched off.

    The house and its earth¶

    The house has a footprint of 10 m × 10 m and stands on a strip foundation whose base lies 0.8 m below ground. The foundation earth electrode (Fundamenterder, DIN 18014) is a round steel bar of 10 mm diameter on the axis of the strip, with 5 cm of concrete all round. It runs as a closed loop under the outer walls. The model house of groundfield's generators (the residential entry of default_building_catalog()) adds one cross-brace each way, for example under inner load-bearing walls: six straight bars of 10 m, 60 m of steel in concrete. DIN 18014 itself asks for cross-braces only where a mesh would exceed 20 m × 20 m; the next section shows what they change.

    The foundation earth electrode is the earth of the house: the main earthing terminal, the protective bonding of the water and gas pipes and, in a TN-C-S system, the earthing of the PEN conductor at the service entrance all connect to it. Three variants, every part bonded to the foundation:

    • A — the foundation earth electrode alone;
    • B — A plus a driven rod, 6 m long, head 0.5 m deep, 1 m in front of the middle of the street-side wall (the service entrance; the black square in the plan below);
    • C — A plus a ring earth electrode, a bare 10 mm steel loop in the soil 1 m outside the foundation (12 m × 12 m, 0.8 m deep). Where the foundation has no contact with the soil (perimeter insulation, waterproof concrete, a bitumen seal), DIN 18014 asks for an earth electrode in the soil instead, typically such a ring, and the steel in the foundation then serves only the equipotential bonding.

    Three soils:

    • S1, homogeneous 100 Ω·m, the reference;
    • S2, 300 Ω·m over 30 Ω·m with the interface 2 m deep: dry sand over a water-bearing layer (reflection factor \(K < 0\));
    • S3, 50 Ω·m over 500 Ω·m with the interface 2 m deep: loam over dry gravel (\(K > 0\)).

    Modelling choices¶

    • A quasi-static field at 50 Hz. The earth of the house spans about 12 m and contains no long conductor. Below 1 kHz the soil behaves as a resistive conductor, so the earth is a resistance \(R_E\). The bonds between the bars are ideal (the generators' default), and the impedance has no imaginary part.
    • Two-layer soil, as a sounding (Wenner, Schlumberger) would give it, solved with the Tagg/Sunde image series of image_2layer, which the default engine selects by itself.
    • The engines. The default image engine (one uniform current per straight wire, exact line-source kernel) gives the resistances. mom (one current per segment) gives the field next to the house, where the image engine warns that its uniform current is only impedance-grade. fem (solid conductors in a meshed soil) is the independent reference. The segments are 0.5 m long: more than five outer radii, as the thin-wire check asks.

    Concrete as a cylindrical shell (ADR-0012, after Sunde). A concrete cover of thickness \(t\) and resistivity \(\rho_c\) around a bar of radius \(r_a\) adds, per metre of bar, the radial resistance

    \[ C = \frac{\rho_c}{2\pi}\,\ln\frac{r_a + t}{r_a} \qquad\text{in }\Omega\cdot\mathrm{m}, \]

    and the soil sees a bare wire of the outer radius \(r_b = r_a + t\) (here 55 mm). If the current leaves the \(L\) metres of encased bar evenly, the shell adds the series resistance \(C/L\). Given concrete_rho_ohm_m, the generators put \(r_b\) and \(C\) on every bar of the foundation, the cross-braces included. ADR-0012 lists fresh or wet concrete at 30 … 80 Ω·m, earth-moist concrete at 80 … 200 Ω·m, concrete in cycling humidity at 200 … 2 000 Ω·m and dry concrete at 5 000 Ω·m and more. The base case takes 150 Ω·m (earth-moist); a sweep covers the rest.

    Copied! 
    import math
import time
import warnings

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

import groundfield as gf
from groundfield.generators import (
    FoundationElectrodeSpec,
    GroundingSystemSpec,
    RodElectrodeSpec,
)
from groundfield.references import ieee80

print("groundfield", gf.__version__)

R_A, COVER, DEPTH, SIDE = 0.005, 0.05, 0.8, 10.0  # m: bar radius, cover, depth, side
RHO_C = 150.0  # Ohm m: earth-moist concrete, the base case
SOILS = {
    "S1": gf.HomogeneousSoil(rho=100.0),
    "S2": gf.TwoLayerSoil(rho_1=300.0, rho_2=30.0, h_1=2.0),
    "S3": gf.TwoLayerSoil(rho_1=50.0, rho_2=500.0, h_1=2.0),
}
ROD = RodElectrodeSpec(length_m=6.0, depth_m=0.5, offset_xy_m=(0.0, -6.0))
RING = FoundationElectrodeSpec(style="ring", size_m=SIDE + 2.0, depth_m=DEPTH)  # bare
VARIANTS = {"A": (), "B": (ROD,), "C": (RING,)}
FOUNDATION = "house_foundation_0"  # the generators' name of the first bar


def house(soil, rho_c=RHO_C, extras=(), style="mesh"):
    # The house earth (foundation plus extras, bonded), fed with 1 A.
    # rho_c=None: the bars lie bare in the soil.
    world = gf.create_world(soil=soil, name="E02 house")
    foundation = FoundationElectrodeSpec(
        style=style,
        size_m=SIDE,
        depth_m=DEPTH,
        wire_radius_m=R_A,
        concrete_rho_ohm_m=rho_c,
        concrete_thickness_m=COVER,
    )
    spec = GroundingSystemSpec(electrodes=[foundation, *extras])
    anchor = spec.build_at(world, (0.0, 0.0), "house", np.random.default_rng(0))
    gf.create_source(world, attached_to=anchor, magnitude=1.0)
    return world


IMAGE = gf.create_engine(segment_length=0.5)  # image_2layer in two layers
MOM = gf.create_engine(backend="mom", segment_length=0.5)


def r_e(world, engine=IMAGE):
    # Earthing resistance in Ohm: the input impedance at 50 Hz.
    return engine.solve(world).input_impedance()[0].real

    Earthing resistance in homogeneous soil¶

    The base case: the foundation earth electrode in earth-moist concrete in 100 Ω·m. Two neighbours help to read the number: the same bars bare in the soil, and the foundation without its two cross-braces. Sverak's formula of IEEE Std 80 (Eq. 57) is a plausibility check; it is an empirical fit for bare substation grids from the total conductor length \(L_T\), the area \(A\) and the depth \(h\),

    \[ R_g = \rho\left[\frac{1}{L_T} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{20A}}\left(1 + \frac{1}{1 + h\sqrt{20/A}}\right)\right], \]

    so it is compared with the bare bars.

    In [4]:
    Copied! 
    s1 = SOILS["S1"]
r_base = r_e(house(s1))
r_bare = r_e(house(s1, rho_c=None))
r_loop = r_e(house(s1, style="ring"))
r_sverak = ieee80.grid_resistance_sverak(
    100.0, total_conductor_length=6 * SIDE, area=SIDE**2, depth=DEPTH
)
print(f"foundation, concrete 150 Ohm m:         R_E = {r_base:.3f} Ohm")
print(f"the same bars bare in the soil:         R_E = {r_bare:.3f} Ohm")
print(f"without the cross-braces, in concrete:  R_E = {r_loop:.3f} Ohm")
print(
    f"IEEE Std 80 (Sverak), bare bars:        R_g = {r_sverak:.3f} Ohm "
    f"({r_sverak / r_bare - 1:+.0%} against the bare bars)"
)

    The house earth has about 5 Ω in 100 Ω·m soil, roughly \(\rho\) / 20 m. Earth-moist concrete adds 7 % to the bare bars. The cross-braces matter more than one might expect: without them the loop alone has 14 % more, because the braces add 50 % to the encased length and spread the current over the area. Sverak's formula lies 18 % above the bare bars, within what an empirical fit for much larger grids can promise.

    How much the concrete matters¶

    The concrete resistivity \(\rho_c\) is the least known input: it follows the moisture of the foundation. The sweep below runs from wet concrete (30 Ω·m) to dry concrete (10 000 Ω·m) in all three soils. The shell resistance \(C/L\) of the 60 m of encased bar is drawn for reference.

    In [6]:
    Copied! 
    rho_c_values = np.array([30, 50, 100, 150, 300, 1000, 3000, 5000, 10000], dtype=float)
C_values = np.array(
    [gf.concrete_shell_coefficient(rc, R_A, COVER) for rc in rho_c_values]
)
shell = C_values / 60.0  # C / L over the 60 m of encased bar
sweep = {
    key: np.array([r_e(house(soil, rho_c=rc)) for rc in rho_c_values])
    for key, soil in SOILS.items()
}
bare = {key: r_e(house(soil, rho_c=None)) for key, soil in SOILS.items()}

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.0))
for k, (key, values) in enumerate(sweep.items()):
    ax.loglog(rho_c_values, values, "o-", color=f"C{k}", label=f"{key}, in concrete")
    ax.axhline(bare[key], color=f"C{k}", ls=":", lw=1)
ax.loglog(rho_c_values, shell, "k--", lw=1, label="shell alone, $C/L$")
ax.set_xlabel(r"concrete resistivity $\rho_c$ in Ω·m")
ax.set_ylabel(r"earthing resistance $R_E$ in Ω")
ax.set_title("Foundation earth electrode (dotted: bars bare in the soil)", fontsize=9)
ax.grid(True, which="both", alpha=0.3)
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout()

print("bars bare in the soil:", {key: round(value, 2) for key, value in bare.items()})
table = pd.DataFrame(sweep, index=pd.Index(rho_c_values, name="rho_c in Ohm m"))
table["C/L"] = shell
table.round(2)

    To separate the shell from the soil, a perfectly conducting shell (\(\rho_c\) = 1 µΩ·m, \(C \approx 0\)) gives the resistance of the thick wire of radius \(r_b\) alone. The rise above it, divided by \(C/L\), should not fall below 1: the shell term is smallest when the current leaves every metre of bar evenly, and the bonded bars choose the distribution with the least total resistance. A dry shell forces that even distribution, so the ratio should approach 1.

    assert np.all(ratio > 1.0 - 1e-9) and np.all(ratio < 1.06)

dry = [values[rho_c_values == 5000.0][0] for values in sweep.values()]
assert max(dry) / min(dry) < 1.10
    assert np.all(ratio > 1.0 - 1e-9) and np.all(ratio < 1.06) assert np.all(np.diff(ratio) < 0) and ratio[-1] < 1.002 # dry: even current # Concrete as resistive as the soil (100 Ohm m in S1) changes nearly nothing. assert abs(sweep["S1"][rho_c_values == 100.0][0] / bare["S1"] - 1.0) < 2e-3 # Dry concrete dominates: the three soils end within 10 % of each other. dry = [values[rho_c_values == 5000.0][0] for values in sweep.values()] assert max(dry) / min(dry) < 1.10

    What the sweep says:

    • Concrete as conductive as the soil changes nothing; wetter concrete lowers \(R_E\) a little, because the soil then sees bars eleven times thicker. In S2, whose top layer (300 Ω·m) is worse than earth-moist concrete, the concrete even improves the earth.
    • Dry concrete dominates. From about \(\rho_c \approx 10\,\rho\) on, the shell term \(C/L\) outgrows the soil part, and at 5 000 Ω·m the earth has 36 … 39 Ω in all three soils: the soil hardly matters any more. Concrete that dries from earth-moist (150 Ω·m) to cycling humidity (1 000 Ω·m) already doubles the earthing resistance.
    • The decomposition holds: the rise above the thick wire is 1.055 \(C/L\) for wet concrete and tends to \(C/L\) for dry concrete, because a dry shell evens out the current over the bars.

    Taking the top layer as homogeneous misjudges the earth by a factor of 2.2 … 2.6 either way: too high over a water-bearing layer (S2), too low over gravel (S3), which is the unsafe side.

    • The foundation feels the soil deep down. Even with the interface 20 m deep, twice the size of the house, the conductive layer still lowers its resistance by 11 % against homogeneous 300 Ω·m (11.67 Ω against 13.07 Ω). A sounding should reach a few times the size of the house.
    • The rod pays off while it reaches the conductive layer (interface above its tip at 6.5 m): it cuts the earthing resistance by 31 … 40 %. Once the good layer lies below the tip, the gain drops to the 6 … 8 % of a rod in the resistive layer.

    • The rod helps where it reaches better soil: −40 % in S2, where it reaches the water-bearing layer, but −8 % in S1 and −2 % in S3, where it ends in gravel.
    • The ring lowers \(R_E\) by 18 … 28 % with moist concrete. Its real value shows with dry concrete: the foundation alone rises to 36 … 39 Ω, while the bare ring in the soil keeps the earth at 4.4 … 6.7 Ω. Where the foundation is insulated or may dry out, the ring is the earth.
    • With dry concrete the rod, too, takes over most of the current and lowers \(R_E\) by 49 … 84 %, because the foundation then leaks so little.

    Potential profile, touch and step voltage¶

    When the earth of the house rises to the earth potential rise \(U_E\), every part bonded to it — the main earthing terminal, the pipes, an outdoor tap, the meter cabinet — rises with it, while the soil outside lies lower. A person standing on the ground 1 m from a touched part bridges the touch voltage \(U_T = U_E - \varphi(\text{feet})\), and a person walking bridges the step voltage between two points 1 m apart (see T08).

    The field is linear in the current. The ratios \(U_T/U_E\) and \(U_S/U_E\) therefore depend only on the geometry and the soil, not on the current nor on what raises the potential: a current that flows through the house earth (\(U_E = R_E I_E\)), or a potential transferred to the house via the PEN conductor from a substation in fault. The feet stand 1 m from the foundation bar, about 0.8 m in front of the façade; the inside of the footprint is not sampled, because there stands the house.

    The image engine warns that its uniform current is only impedance-grade next to a bonded cluster of wires, so the field is computed with mom (the engines section below quantifies the difference).

    In [15]:
    Copied! 
    def field(soil, rho_c=RHO_C, extras=()):
    # mom solution and its earth potential rise per ampere.
    world = house(soil, rho_c=rho_c, extras=extras)
    result = MOM.solve(world)
    return world, result, result.input_impedance()[0].real


def surface(result, x, y):
    # Surface potential at the points (x, y), in V per A.
    pts = np.column_stack([np.ravel(x), np.ravel(y), np.zeros(np.size(x))])
    return result.potential(pts).real.reshape(np.shape(x))

    Under the house the ground stays at about 0.8 \(U_E\) with moist concrete: the foundation grades the potential of the floor, which is why it serves as protective bonding as well as an earth. Outside, the potential falls steeply: at the feet 1 m out, 40 % of the earth potential rise is gone in front of the middle of a wall and about half at a corner (the map). The ring 1 m outside lifts the potential exactly where people stand (0.81 instead of 0.60 \(U_E\) in front of the wall). With dry concrete the shell takes up most of the voltage, and the soil around the house hardly rises at all (0.08 \(U_E\) at the feet): the bonded parts are at \(U_E\) while the ground is close to remote earth.

    The table collects, for every soil and variant (moist concrete) and for dry concrete in S1:

    • \(R_E\) from mom;
    • the largest touch voltage on the curve 1 m from the bars (gf.touch_voltage_envelope, 72 directions), as a fraction of \(U_E\) and per ampere of earth current;
    • the largest step voltage, as a fraction of \(U_E\), from the foundation line outwards along the axis and the diagonal of the house.
    In [17]:
    Copied! 
    def assess(soil, rho_c=RHO_C, extras=()):
    world, result, u_e = field(soil, rho_c=rho_c, extras=extras)
    _, u_t = gf.touch_voltage_envelope(result, world, electrode=FOUNDATION, n_angles=72)
    u_s = 0.0
    for start, d in ((5.0, (1.0, 0.0)), (5.0 * math.sqrt(2.0), (1.0, 1.0))):
        d = np.array(d) / np.hypot(*d)
        r = np.arange(start, 30.0, 0.05)
        phi = surface(result, r * d[0], r * d[1])
        phi_1m = surface(result, (r + 1.0) * d[0], (r + 1.0) * d[1])
        u_s = max(u_s, np.max(phi - phi_1m))
    u_t_max = np.max(np.abs(u_t))
    return {
        "R_E": u_e,
        "U_T/U_E": u_t_max / u_e,
        "U_T/I_E": u_t_max,  # V per A of earth current
        "U_S/U_E": u_s / u_e,
    }

u_s_scan = surface(result, 5.0, 0.0) - surface(result, 6.0, 0.0)
assert abs(u_s_helper - u_s_scan) < 1e-9
    ratio_t = safety["U_T/U_E"] by_variant = {v: ratio_t.xs(v, level="variant") for v in VARIANTS} assert np.all(by_variant["C"] < 0.65 * by_variant["A"]) assert ratio_t[("S1 dry", "A")] > 0.9 # dry concrete: almost the full EPR assert ratio_t[("S2", "A")] > ratio_t[("S1", "A")] > ratio_t[("S3", "A")] assert np.all(safety["U_S/U_E"] < safety["U_T/U_E"]) # The rod lowers R_E, hardly the ratio; per ampere it still helps. assert abs(ratio_t[("S1", "B")] / ratio_t[("S1", "A")] - 1.0) < 0.05 assert safety.loc[("S2", "B"), "U_T/I_E"] < 0.7 * safety.loc[("S2", "A"), "U_T/I_E"] # One point of the scan with the library's own step-voltage helper: world, result, u_e = field(SOILS["S1"]) u_s_helper = gf.step_voltage( result, position=(5.0, 0.0, 0.0), direction=(1.0, 0.0, 0.0) ) u_s_scan = surface(result, 5.0, 0.0) - surface(result, 6.0, 0.0) assert abs(u_s_helper - u_s_scan) < 1e-9

    How to read the table:

    • Touch voltage. With the foundation alone, about half the earth potential rise appears as touch voltage in S1; in S2, whose resistive top layer lets the current dive to the conductive layer, almost three quarters; in S3, whose conductive top layer spreads it sideways, under a third. The ring lowers the ratio to a third … three fifths of its value without it. The rod leaves the ratio almost unchanged: it lowers \(R_E\), so it helps where a current sets the earth potential rise (the column per ampere: −42 % in S2), not where a potential is transferred.
    • Dry concrete raises the ratio to 0.93: the touch voltage is then practically the full earth potential rise, and per ampere 13 times that of the moist foundation. The ring brings it back to 0.31.
    • Step voltages stay below the touch voltages, with their largest values just outside the foundation bars (or outside the ring).

    What the touch voltages allow¶

    EN 50522 limits the touch voltage \(U_{Tp}\) by the fault duration \(t_f\) (Table B.4: 225 V at 0.5 s; 80 V beyond 10 s and for an earth fault that is not cleared). It applies to earth faults in high-voltage installations; a house in a TN network meets them as a potential transferred via the PEN conductor. The low-voltage installation itself has its own rules (IEC 60364-4-41). The ratio \(U_T/U_E\) turns \(U_{Tp}\) into the largest earth potential rise the house can carry without extra measures, \(U_{E,\max} = U_{Tp} / (U_T/U_E)\):

}

    A foundation earth electrode in moist concrete lets the house carry roughly twice \(U_{Tp}\) as earth potential rise (S1: 439 V for a fault cleared in 0.5 s, 156 V for one that is not cleared); the ring outside doubles that again. Over the water-bearing layer of S2 and with dry concrete the margin shrinks towards \(U_{Tp}\) itself. In a real TN network the neighbouring house earths and the substation raise the soil around the house as well, which lowers the touch voltage further; for the touch voltage this single house is the pessimistic end (see the case study E01 of a secondary substation with its low-voltage network).

    The engines compared¶

    image against mom on the house¶

    The image engine carries one uniform leakage current per straight bar and integrates the line source exactly. mom gives every 0.5 m segment its own current, so the current can crowd towards the corners and ends of the bars, but evaluates each segment as a point source. The cell compares \(R_E\) and the touch-voltage ratio of variants A and C, moist concrete, in the three soils, and records the warning of the image engine.

The feet stand right above the ring, where the surface potential depends on how the current is distributed along each side; in reality it crowds towards the corners, the image engine keeps it uniform per side. The error is on the safe side here, but it is the reason for the warning: for the field next to bonded clusters, grids, stars and strip ends, use mom (tutorial T08).

    The segment length¶

    The image engine's line kernel integrates every straight bar exactly, so a square foundation gives the same resistance at every segment length. mom converges with the segment length:

    fem on a ring analogue (axisymmetric model)¶

    fem meshes the soil and treats each electrode as the solid body it is: a rod as a cylinder, a ring as a torus, the concrete shell as a surface conductance \(1/(2\pi r_b C)\) on the surface of radius \(r_b\). Its axisymmetric model solves rods on one vertical axis and rings around it to about \(10^{-4}\), in a fraction of a second. A square foundation is not axisymmetric, so we take a ring analogue: a circular ring with the same 40 m of encased bar as the foundation loop without cross-braces (radius \(40\,\mathrm{m}/2\pi\) = 6.37 m, 0.8 m deep) in earth-moist concrete, in the three soils. The shell rise is measured against the same ring with a perfectly conducting shell (\(C = 0\)).

    In [25]:
    Copied! 
    R_RING = 4.0 * SIDE / (2.0 * math.pi)
C_LOOP = C_150 / (2.0 * math.pi * R_RING)  # the shell term C / L of the ring


def ring_analogue(soil, shell=True):
    # Circular ring of radius r_b = 55 mm; shell=False: C = 0.
    world = gf.create_world(soil=soil, name="E02 ring analogue")
    gf.create_electrode(
        world,
        "ring",
        name="ring",
        center=(0.0, 0.0, DEPTH),
        radius=R_RING,
        wire_radius=R_A + COVER,
        concrete_shell_coefficient_ohm_m=C_150 if shell else 0.0,
    )
    gf.create_source(world, attached_to="ring", magnitude=1.0)
    return world


FEM = gf.create_engine(backend="fem", segment_length=0.5)  # axisymmetric here
ENGINES = {"image": IMAGE, "mom": MOM, "fem": FEM}
rows, timing = {}, {}
with warnings.catch_warnings():
    # fem is experimental and says so once per process.
    warnings.simplefilter("ignore", gf.ExperimentalBackendWarning)
    for key, soil in SOILS.items():
        world, z, ratio = ring_analogue(soil), {}, {}
        for name, eng in ENGINES.items():
            t0 = time.perf_counter()
            res = eng.solve(world)
            timing[name] = time.perf_counter() - t0
            z[name] = res.input_impedance()[0].real
            ratio[name] = abs(gf.touch_voltage(res, world, electrode="ring")) / z[name]
        fem_thick = r_e(ring_analogue(soil, shell=False), FEM)
        rows[key] = {
            "R_E fem": z["fem"],
            "image/fem-1": z["image"] / z["fem"] - 1.0,
            "mom/fem-1": z["mom"] / z["fem"] - 1.0,
            "fem rise/(C/L)": (z["fem"] - fem_thick) / C_LOOP,
            "U_T image/fem-1": ratio["image"] / ratio["fem"] - 1.0,
        }
ring_table = pd.DataFrame(rows).T
ring_table.round(5)

    Three independent methods, one ring:

    • image agrees with fem to a few \(10^{-4}\), in resistance and in touch voltage. On a ring the uniform current is exact by symmetry, so the only difference left is the image engine's polygon of 0.5 m chords, which lies slightly inside the circle.
    • mom lies 0.3 … 1.9 % below. Its point kernel represents each segment's current by a point source at the segment's midpoint, which reads the resistance low; this deficit does not vanish as the segments get shorter (tutorial T09).
    • The shell model is consistent. The image engine adds exactly \(C/L\); fem adds 0.1 … 0.2 % more, because on the solid torus the current is not spread evenly around the wire's circumference, and an uneven current loses more in the shell.

    fem on the real foundation (three-dimensional model)¶

    Every other world — the square loop, the braces, the rod beside the foundation — needs the three-dimensional model of fem. It replaces each wire by a line source smoothed over a disc of radius source_radius, meshes the soil with tetrahedra and corrects for the wire radius analytically. It needs the optional fem3d extra and is expensive: the foundation loop without cross-braces (40 m of bar, S1, moist concrete), with a 0.1 m source radius and the mesh growth 0.6, has 1.04 million nodes on its finer mesh level. On the machine that executed this notebook it took one to three minutes, depending on what else was running, and up to 3.5 GB of memory. The cell below runs it only on request and otherwise uses the value of that run.

    The image engine lies 0.4 … 2.2 % above mom on the house and overestimates the touch voltage over the ring by up to 16 % (see above); that is why the field near the house comes from mom.

    The pair image and mom brackets the solid-conductor value of fem from above and below: the uniform current per wire overestimates the resistance, the point kernel underestimates it. For an engineering answer both are good to about 2 %, far below the uncertainty of the concrete and the soil.

    What this means in practice¶

    • A foundation earth electrode of a 10 m × 10 m house has about \(\rho\) / 20 m in homogeneous soil (5.0 Ω in 100 Ω·m) as long as the concrete is moist.
    • The concrete is neutral while it is about as conductive as the soil; dry concrete multiplies the earthing resistance (about 36 Ω at 5 000 Ω·m) and makes the soil irrelevant.
    • The soil model matters as much: the homogeneous soil of the top layer misjudges the earth by a factor of 2.2 … 2.6 either way, and the foundation still feels a layer 20 m down. Use a sounding that reaches a few times the size of the house.
    • A driven rod pays off when it reaches a better layer (−40 % in S2); it lowers \(R_E\) but not the touch voltage as a fraction of the earth potential rise.
    • A ring earth electrode 1 m outside lowers \(R_E\), cuts the touch voltage around the house by 40 … 67 % and keeps the earth working when the foundation dries out or is insulated.
    • Engines: image for resistances and sweeps, mom for the field next to the house, fem to confirm a result once; they agree within about 2 %.

    Limits of this example¶

    • One house alone. In a TN network the house is bonded through the PEN to the substation and to every other house; the global earthing system lowers both the earthing impedance seen at the house and the touch voltages around it (case study E01).
    • The concrete model is a cylindrical shell of uniform resistivity around each bar. The real strip foundation is a block of concrete several times wider than the shell; DIN 18014 bonds the bar to the reinforcement at least every 2 m, which enlarges the electrode; and the moisture varies over the foundation and the year. Where bars meet, their shells overlap; the concrete-shells page estimates that this changes the house mesh by about 1 % or less.
    • The soil is horizontally layered and uniform in each layer: no backfill around the foundation, no frost, no seasonal moisture profile.
    • Touch voltages are prospective: no body, shoe or surface-layer resistance (EN 50522, Annex B, and gf.permissible_prospective_touch_voltage_en50522 add them). The feet stand 1 m from the bars; touched parts farther out (a bonded fence, a garden tap on a pipe) carry the house potential to places where the soil lies lower and need their own assessment with gf.touch_voltage_at_part.
    • Frequency: 50 Hz, no inductive conductor in the model; harmonics and lightning currents are outside its scope.
    • The 3-D fem reference was run once for the loop without braces in S1; the other worlds rest on the agreement of image and mom and on the axisymmetric ring analogue.
